title: A 3,000-Year-Old City Gets a Superhero Shield!
summary: Imagine walking through a city where kings and prophets lived 3,000 years ago. That's Sebastia, an amazing archaeological site in the West Bank. It has Roman columns, an ancient amphitheater (a big outdoor theater), and even the tomb of John the Baptist! But this old city is in big trouble. Israel wants to take over about 180 hectares (that's like 250 soccer fields!) of land around it. They say it's to "preserve and develop" the area. But Palestinian leaders and people who live there say it's really a land grab that will hurt their homes and businesses. Many families depend on tourists visiting the ruins to make a living. Now, UNESCO (a United Nations group that protects important places around the world) has stepped in. On Friday, they added Sebastia to the World Heritage list AND the list of World Heritage in Danger. That's like giving it a double shield! Palestinian officials are cheering. Nizar Kayed, the deputy mayor of Sebastia, said the Israeli plan "destroys this area from a cultural and historical standpoint and also destroys people's livelihoods." But Israel is not happy. They say the UNESCO decision is just political, not about protecting history. Will the UNESCO listing actually stop Israel? Maybe not. In 2017, UNESCO added Hebron's Old City to the same list, but Israel still kept settlers there and took over a mosque. Still, Palestinians hope this new title will bring more attention and help save the ancient stones and olive trees of Sebastia.
why_it_matters: Ancient places like Sebastia teach us about our history and belong to all of us; when they are threatened, we risk losing the stories of our ancestors and the chance to understand where we come from.

background_read: Sebastia, also known as Samaria, was an important city in biblical times. It was the capital of the ancient Northern Kingdom of Israel around 900 BC. Later, the Romans built huge structures there, including the amphitheater.

The West Bank is a landlocked territory where both Israelis and Palestinians live, though most of the world considers it Palestinian land occupied by Israel since 1967. Many historical sites in the West Bank are at the centre of disputes.

UNESCO (the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) is a UN agency that names World Heritage sites to protect places of outstanding value to humanity. When a site is in danger, UNESCO adds it to a special list to call for international help.
